summary: This document defines a YANG data model to configure and manage OSPF. It is based on YANG 1.1 as defined in RFC 7950 and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture described in RFC 8342.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF is how routers share maps of the network. This document defines a standard form for configuring it and viewing its state.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 routers and reading their state.

tldr.problem: OSPF configuration differs from vendor to vendor, in how a protocol instance is tied to a routing domain and how multiple instances are created, so tools cannot manage routers in one common way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9129 defines the ietf-ospf YANG module. It augments the core routing model with one OSPF container for configuration and operational state, covering both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, with optional features, notifications and two RPC operations.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get a common interface (over NETCONF, RESTCONF or other protocols) that vendors can extend with their own additions.

today: RFC 9129 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Model Is For
sections.content:
YANG (RFC 7950) is a data definition language used to define the contents of a conceptual datastore, so networked devices can be managed with NETCONF (RFC 6241), RESTCONF (RFC 8040) and other protocols. Models can also back command-line interfaces and programmatic APIs.

RFC 9129 defines a YANG data model to configure and manage OSPF. It augments the core routing data model of RFC 8349, refers to interfaces through the interface model of RFC 8343, and uses the key chain model of RFC 8177 for authentication. It fully conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). Both OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) are supported, along with a set of optional features from other OSPF RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers speak to each other with a protocol called OSPF. This document gives people one common set of buttons and dials to control it, whatever brand of router they have.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The basics of OSPF configuration (routers, areas, interfaces) are the same everywhere, but the detailed configuration model varies among vendors. The goal is a user interface common to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. Very little is marked mandatory, which leaves vendors freedom to fit the model to their products.

Operational state lives in the same tree as configuration, as the NMDA expects. So only the routing container of the ietf-routing model is augmented, and the older routing-state container is not. A mandatory version field says whether an instance is OSPFv2 or OSPFv3, and the model adapts to the differences between them.
sections.plainLanguage: All stores sell the same kinds of things, but arrange them in different ways. The goal is one arrangement that works for both versions of the game and leaves each store room to add its own touches.

sections.title: Where the Module Sits in the Tree
sections.content:
The ietf-ospf module augments /routing/control-plane-protocols/control-plane-protocol from the ietf-routing module with an ospf container. That container is a single OSPF instance, which can be OSPFv2 or OSPFv3. Several instances are created as several control-plane protocol instances, each mapping to one instance as defined in RFC 8349.

Inside the instance, the areas container holds a list of areas, and each area has its own interfaces. An area can also have virtual-links and, with the pe-ce-protocol feature, sham-links. A topologies container appears when the multi-topology feature is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a family tree: the router is the trunk, areas are big branches, and interfaces are the small twigs on each branch.

sections.title: Optional Features
sections.content:
Beyond basic OSPF, the model defines optional YANG features. Each vendor decides whether to support a feature on a given device, and the RFC expects vendors to add more through their own augmentations. Examples include multi-topology routing, multi-area adjacencies, demand circuits, link-local signaling, graceful restart, non-stop routing, IP fast reroute with loop-free alternates, BFD, stub router advertisements and OSPF as a PE-CE protocol.

Several features cover authentication: the OSPFv2 authentication trailer, IPsec for OSPFv3, and the OSPFv3 authentication trailer. There are also tuning features such as auto-cost for reference-bandwidth cost calculation, max-ecmp for the maximum number of equal-cost paths, max-lsa for the maximum number of LSAs accepted, and ietf-spf-delay for the IETF SPF delay algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The base kit has the basic parts. Extra pieces are sold separately, and each store chooses which ones to stock.

sections.title: Router, Area and Interface State
sections.content:
The model has three levels, each with configuration and read-only operational state. At the router level (the ospf container) the operational state includes instance statistics, IETF SPF delay statistics, the AS-scope link state database (LSDB), the local RIB, the SPF log and the LSA log.

At the area level, the state includes area statistics and the area LSDB, and the configuration covers things like the area type, summary behavior, default cost and address ranges. At the interface level, the state includes interface statistics, the list of neighbors and the link-local LSDB. Interface configuration covers the interface type, hello, dead, retransmit and transmit-delay values, cost, authentication, and options such as passive mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps a notebook for the whole network, a smaller notebook for each neighborhood, and a tiny note for each street. Each has settings you can change and facts you can only read.

sections.title: Notifications and RPC Operations
sections.content:
The module defines notifications that tell YANG clients about important events. They cover the common set of traps from the OSPFv2 MIB (RFC 4750) and OSPFv3 MIB (RFC 5643). Examples are if-state-change, nbr-state-change, if-config-error, if-rx-bad-packet, lsdb-approaching-overflow, lsdb-overflow, nssa-translator-status-change and restart-status-change.

It also defines two RPC operations. clear-database resets the contents of a particular OSPF LSDB, forces neighbor adjacencies to the DOWN state, and re-originates self-originated LSAs. clear-neighbor resets a particular OSPF neighbor or a group of neighbors associated with an OSPF interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can ring a bell when something important happens. You can also press two reset buttons: one that makes it forget what it has learned and start over, and one that makes it forget a particular neighbor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed over NETCONF (secure transport: SSH) or RESTCONF (secure transport: TLS), and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can limit what each user may do. The RFC lists the writable subtrees as sensitive. Changing OSPF configuration can compromise the whole OSPF domain, for example by adding OSPF to an unprotected interface so an unauthorized neighbor forms an adjacency, or by setting asymmetric interface costs to cause a routing loop.

The readable LSDB subtrees are sensitive too, since exposing them reveals the detailed network topology, and in an area LSDB the complete IP and TE topology can be reconstructed. For authentication, key chains are RECOMMENDED over locally specified keys because of seamless key and algorithm rollover, hexadecimal keys with more entropy, and encryption of keys with AES Key Wrap with Padding. The clear-neighbor and clear-database RPCs can be used for denial of service if access is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel is powerful, so only trusted people should hold the keys. Someone who gets in could redirect traffic or see a map of the whole network.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ospf in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant contact. It also registers the YANG module ietf-ospf in the YANG Module Names registry (RFC 6020), with the namespace above, the prefix ospf and a reference to RFC 9129.
sections.plainLanguage: The model gets its own official name tag in a public list, so nobody else uses the same name for something different.
